title: Ricketts v. Scothorn
summary: A grandfather’s gratuitous $2,000 note, given so that his granddaughter would no longer have to work, was enforceable against his estate: although her quitting was not the bargained-for price of the note, he intentionally induced her to change her position in reliance on it, so equitable estoppel barred the executor from pleading want of consideration.

sections.Parties: Katie Scothorn, John C. Ricketts’s granddaughter and a bookkeeper who left her job after receiving his note, was the plaintiff and defendant in error; she obtained judgment on the note. Andrew D. Ricketts, executor of John C. Ricketts’s estate, was the defendant and plaintiff in error, resisting enforcement for want of consideration. Justice Sullivan wrote for the Supreme Court of Nebraska on December 8, 1898.
sections.Material Facts: On May 1, 1891 John C. Ricketts signed a note promising to pay Katie Scothorn $2,000 on demand with six percent annual interest. She was then a bookkeeper for Mayer Brothers earning $10 a week. Around nine that morning he visited her at the store, took the note from his vest, and told her he had fixed things so she would not have to work any more, adding that none of his other grandchildren worked and she need not either. She took the note, kissed him, cried, and soon gave up the position. She stayed out of work for more than a year; in September 1892, with his consent, she took a bookkeeping job with Funke & Ogden. He paid one year’s interest, said he would pay the note when he sold his Ohio farm, and never repudiated it. He died on June 8, 1894.
sections.Procedural History: Scothorn sued the executor on the note in the District Court of Lancaster County, alleging that Ricketts gave it to induce her to give up her job and that she relied on it for support. The executor denied the allegations and pleaded want of consideration. The material facts were undisputed at trial and Scothorn recovered judgment. The executor brought error to the Nebraska Supreme Court, challenging the note’s admission, the sufficiency of consideration and the treatment of the undisputed evidence. The court held that equitable estoppel barred the defense as a matter of law, treated any trial error as harmless because only one result was possible, and affirmed.
sections.Issue: When a grandfather gives his working granddaughter a gratuitous promissory note while reasonably contemplating that she will leave her job, and she does leave in reliance on the note, may his executor assert lack of consideration to defeat enforcement?
sections.Holding: No. The note was a promised gift: Ricketts requested no return performance and Scothorn made no bargained-for promise, so ordinary consideration was lacking. But he intentionally influenced her to alter her position for the worse on the faith of the note, in a way he could reasonably foresee, and equitable estoppel therefore precluded his executor from asserting want of consideration. The judgment enforcing the note was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Consideration requires a performance or return promise sought in exchange for the promisor’s commitment. Ricketts imposed no condition and asked for nothing; he meant to give his granddaughter financial independence, leaving her free to work or not, so her resignation was a consequence of the gift promise rather than its price. The court then turned to the charitable-subscription cases; those opinions often called the induced expenditure consideration, but the real principle at work was equitable estoppel. Estoppel in pais arises from conduct that induces another to change position in accordance with the actor’s real or apparent intention, and it precludes the actor from later asserting a right against the person who relied in good faith and changed position for the worse. Ricketts tied the note directly to Scothorn’s freedom from work; her resignation was a reasonable and probable response to his words and the promised income; she gave up a $10-a-week position. Her later return to work did not undo reliance that had already occurred. The case predates § 90 and reaches, through estoppel language, what later writers called promissory estoppel.

priorVersions.summary: The grandfather induced a change of position without bargaining for it; the court used estoppel to prevent the estate from invoking lack of consideration.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Supreme Court of Nebraska (1898).

The casebook next traces the move from equitable estoppel, commonly involving a representation of fact, to promissory estoppel based on an assurance of future conduct. It also compares land improvements, bailments, and charitable subscriptions.

sections.Parties: Katie Scothorn sought payment of her grandfather’s note from Ricketts, the executor of his estate.
sections.Material Facts: The grandfather gave Scothorn a $2,000 note bearing interest and told her that she would no longer need to work. She had been earning $10 per week as a bookkeeper and quit her job. He had not required her to quit as the price of the promise. She later returned to work with his approval. The dispute arose against the estate.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered judgment for Scothorn. The Supreme Court of Nebraska affirmed, using the grandfather’s inducement of reliance to prevent the lack-of-consideration defense.
sections.Issue: Could the note be enforced when leaving work was a foreseeable and induced change of position but was not requested in exchange for it?
sections.Holding: The court held the estate estopped to deny enforceability on that ground. It did not characterize the gift promise as an ordinary bargained-for exchange.
sections.Reasoning: The crucial distinction is between a condition of a bargain and an action induced by an unconditional promise. Scothorn’s departure from work was not consideration, because the grandfather had not sought it as the price of payment. Nevertheless, allowing him or his estate to retract the promise after inducing that change would permit the injustice the court’s estoppel analysis addresses.

learning.why: Ricketts makes the difference between an act requested as payment and an act foreseeably induced by a promise visible. The same act can matter in different ways depending on the promise’s terms.

topics.promissory-estoppel: The gift promise induced the change of position supporting enforcement.
topics.consideration: The court expressly finds no requested exchange.
topics.reliance: Leaving an existing job was the change caused by the assurance.
